reason:
Attacked and it holds. Raw wikitext of the scan-backed page en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Jade_Mountain.djvu/114 prints THE HARD ROAD with the sub-heading (Written to Music), and the poem ends on that page with exactly the two lines proposed, immediately after the refrain 'Journeying is hard, / Journeying is hard. / There are many turnings— / Which am I to follow?': 'I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.' Character for character, both line heads capitalised as in the edition, and it is genuinely the closing couplet, not a couplet pulled from the middle. The running-folio template at the foot of the page renders 70, so the printed page is 70 and 114 is the djvu sequence, exactly as the evidence states.
Attribution attacked two ways and confirmed twice. The Wikisource mainspace header for The Jade Mountain/The Hard Road carries section_author = Li Bai, translator1 = Witter Bynner, translator2 = Jiang Kanghu, with previous = Endless Yearning and next = Bringing in the Wine, which is the Li Po sequence. Independently, the facing scan page djvu/113 (printed 69) carries the running head 'Li Po' and prints ENDLESS YEARNING, so THE HARD ROAD falls inside Li Po's section with no intervening poet heading. Li Bai is not banned and stands at 0 of 3 under both Li Bai and Li Po; shipped.js returns no hit and no near hit.
Everything else checks. 1929 edition, in scope, Poetry is the form of the work. Source line is 93 characters, leads with the name, carries no dash, and puts the translation in parentheses last. Verse lineation preserved, ends in a full stop, no straight double quote. On theme it is the road poem of the batch, and taken as the closing couplet it lifts rather than sinks, which matters for six in the morning: the despair is in the lines above it, the resolve is in these two. Publishable.
One inconsistency worth fixing, not a refutation: the note is empty, while its sibling 04-poet-07 notes that the 1929 edition prints the poet under an older romanisation. The same is true here, the book prints Li Po, and the two cards will sit in the same month from the same book. Give this one a matching one-line note saying the 1929 edition prints the poet as Li Po, so the pair reads consistently.
